slides: Open by making the triangle feel like a laboratory rather than a familiar picture. The chapter starts from primitive Euclidean claims, then turns each claim into an inspectable invariant: preserved lengths, concurrent medians, equal distances, collinearity, circle radii, optimization witnesses, and trisector surprises.

Use this route slide to keep the lecture from becoming a catalog of named centers. The order is conceptual: first preserve geometry under reflection, then compare affine and metric centers, then watch the Euler line organize later constructions, and finally test optimization and Morley phenomena.

The reflection visual grounds congruence in measurement. A mirror map is an isometry, so corresponding side lengths and base angles must match. The important teaching move is that symmetry is not accepted by sight alone; the figure is paired with numerical preservation errors near machine precision.

The centroid slide separates affine geometry from metric geometry. Medians use only midpoint and straight-line structure, and the centroid is the average of the vertices. The two-to-one ratios survive shape changes because this construction does not depend on angles or side lengths.

This comparison prevents the common mistake of treating all triangle centers alike. The incenter is controlled by equal distances to side lines, while the circumcenter is controlled by equal distances to vertices. One center is tangent to the sides; the other sees the vertices on a circle.

The Euler line and nine-point circle give the chapter its organizing drama. The vector identity says more than a ruler drawing: the orthocenter, centroid, and circumcenter are locked into a two-to-one relation. The nine-point circle then packages midpoint and altitude-foot constructions into one radius check.

The extremum problems show how classical geometry can hide optimization. Fagnano asks for a shortest inscribed triangle and lands on the orthic triangle for an acute triangle. Fermat asks for the shortest total distance to the vertices and produces the interior one hundred twenty degree condition.

Morley's theorem is intentionally surprising because angle trisectors usually warn students about difficult constructions. Here the intersections of adjacent trisectors form an equilateral triangle. The slide should emphasize measured side equality and sixty degree angles rather than relying on the visual surprise alone.

The dependency map turns proof structure into a navigable object. It tells students which constructions must be trusted before later facts make sense, and the symbolic Euler check complements the floating-point drawings by proving the key collinearity identity exactly for a rational triangle.

Close by recasting the chapter as a method. A theorem becomes durable when the diagram, a local invariant, and a numerical or symbolic check agree. Triangles remain central because they let congruence, centers, lines, circles, extrema, and unexpected trisectors all be tested in one small setting.
